'''Amy Susanne Gladfelter''' is a quantitative cell biologist interested in fundamental mechanisms of cell organization.  She is currently a Distinguished Duke Health Science and Technology Professor<ref>{{Cite web |title=Amy Susanne Gladfelter {{!}} Scholars@Duke profile |url=https://scholars.duke.edu/person/Amy.Gladfelter |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=scholars.duke.edu |language=en}}</ref>  in the Cell Biology and Biomedical Engineering Departments at [[Duke University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Duke University |url=https://www.duke.edu/ |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=Duke University |language=en-US}}</ref>  Previously, she was Professor of Biology and Associate chair at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Homepage |url=https://bio.unc.edu/ |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=UNC DEPARTMENT OF BIOLOGY |language=en-US}}</ref> from 2016–2023.  She remains a longstanding fellow of the [https://www.mbl.edu/ Marine Biological Laboratory] in [[Woods Hole, Massachusetts]] and is currently the director of the Physiology Course.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physiology: Modern Cell Biology Using Microscopic, Biochemical and Computational Approaches {{!}} Marine Biological Laboratory |url=https://www.mbl.edu/education/advanced-research-training-courses/course-offerings/physiology-modern-cell-biology-using-microscopic-biochemical-and-computational-approaches |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=www.mbl.edu |language=en}}</ref> In her research program, she uses [[microscopy]], biophysical and genetic approaches to study [[Syncytium|syncytial cells]].  

==Education==
She trained at [[Princeton University]] (AB) with [[Bonnie Bassler]], Duke University (Ph.D.) with Danny Lew and [[University of Basel|UniBasel]] Biozentrum (post-doc) with Peter Philippsen before starting her independent career at [[Dartmouth College|Dartmouth]] in the Biological Sciences<ref>{{Cite web |title=Department of Biological Sciences |url=https://biology.dartmouth.edu/ |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=Department of Biological Sciences |language=en}}</ref> department in 2006, where she worked until 2016. She has been honored with the 2014 Graduate Mentoring Award from Dartmouth, the 2015 Mid-Career Award for Excellence in Research from the [[American Society for Cell Biology|American Society of Cell Biology]], the 2020 Graduate school mentoring award from UNC and was a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] Faculty Scholar.  She is an elected fellow of the [[American Society for Microbiology|America Academy for Microbiology]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].

==Cell biology research==
Gladfelter’s research is focused on the form and function of syncytial cells<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Keenen |first=Madeline M. |last2=Jalihal |first2=Ameya |last3=Gladfelter |first3=Amy S. |date=June 2025 |title=Achieving multifunctionality in a single, tissue-sized syncytiotrophoblast cell in humans |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0143400425002097 |journal=Placenta |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.placenta.2025.06.004|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jalihal |first=Ameya P. |last2=Gladfelter |first2=Amy S. |date=June 2025 |title=Fungal syncytia |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0960982225001174 |journal=Current Biology |language=en |volume=35 |issue=11 |pages=R490–R495 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2025.01.054}}</ref> where many nuclei share a common cytoplasm. She uses biophysical, imaging and modeling approaches in filamentous fungi and placenta to learn the biology of these systems and uncover general principles of cell organization. 

Her research program began trying to solve a puzzle of [[cell cycle]] regulation which was how nuclei can divide out of sync with one another in a common cytoplasm<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gladfelter |first=Amy S. |last2=Hungerbuehler |first2=A. Katrin |last3=Philippsen |first3=Peter |date=January 30, 2006 |title=Asynchronous nuclear division cycles in multinucleated cells |url=https://rupress.org/jcb/article/172/3/347/44135/Asynchronous-nuclear-division-cycles-in |journal=The Journal of Cell Biology |language=en |volume=172 |issue=3 |pages=347–362 |doi=10.1083/jcb.200507003 |issn=1540-8140|pmc=2063645 }}</ref>. This suggested some form of local regulation of the cell cycle.  Her group found local control emerges from RNA-based condensates that restrict diffusion of [[cyclin]] transcripts and promote nuclear individuality so nuclei can divide independently of neighboring nuclei sharing a cytoplasm<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=ChangHwan |last2=Zhang |first2=Huaiying |last3=Baker |first3=Amy E. |last4=Occhipinti |first4=Patricia |last5=Borsuk |first5=Mark E. |last6=Gladfelter |first6=Amy S. |title=Protein Aggregation Behavior Regulates Cyclin Transcript Localization and Cell-Cycle Control |journal=Developmental Cell |date=June 24, 2013 |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=572–584 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2013.05.007 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016%2Fj.devcel.2013.05.007 |language=English |issn=1534-5807|pmc=4113091 }}</ref>.  Since that observation, which was one of the early roles described for condensates, she has been using this system and others to understand how RNA sequences and structures can control the molecular composition, identity and function of condensates<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roden |first=Christine |last2=Gladfelter |first2=Amy S. |date=March 2021 |title=RNA contributions to the form and function of biomolecular condensates |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41580-020-0264-6 |journal=Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology |language=en |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=183–195 |doi=10.1038/s41580-020-0264-6 |issn=1471-0072|pmc=7785677 }}</ref> .  These studies extended to the RNA condensates in SARS CoV-2<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iserman |first=Christiane |last2=Roden |first2=Christine A. |last3=Boerneke |first3=Mark A. |last4=Sealfon |first4=Rachel S.G. |last5=McLaughlin |first5=Grace A. |last6=Jungreis |first6=Irwin |last7=Fritch |first7=Ethan J. |last8=Hou |first8=Yixuan J. |last9=Ekena |first9=Joanne |last10=Weidmann |first10=Chase A. |last11=Theesfeld |first11=Chandra L. |last12=Kellis |first12=Manolis |last13=Troyanskaya |first13=Olga G. |last14=Baric |first14=Ralph S. |last15=Sheahan |first15=Timothy P. |date=December 2020 |title=Genomic RNA Elements Drive Phase Separation of the SARS-CoV-2 Nucleocapsid |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1097276520308418 |journal=Molecular Cell |language=en |volume=80 |issue=6 |pages=1078–1091.e6 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2020.11.041|pmc=7691212 }}</ref>, which also induces syncytial cells, and now the enormous syncytiotrophoblast cells of placenta<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Keenen |first=Madeline M |last2=Yang |first2=Liheng |last3=Liang |first3=Huan |last4=Farmer |first4=Veronica J |last5=Worota |first5=Rizban E |last6=Singh |first6=Rohit |last7=Gladfelter |first7=Amy S |last8=Coyne |first8=Carolyn B |date=May 27, 2025 |title=Comparative analysis of the syncytiotrophoblast in placenta tissue and trophoblast organoids using snRNA sequencing |url=https://elifesciences.org/articles/101170 |journal=eLife |language=en |volume=13 |doi=10.7554/eLife.101170  |doi-access=free|issn=2050-084X|pmc=12113261 }}</ref>. 

In a second area of work, she had studied how the septin [[cytoskeleton]] influences the shape of large syncytial cells.  She has implemented new imaging techniques and developed innovative reconstitution assays to study septin filament dynamics on membranes<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bridges |first=Andrew A. |last2=Jentzsch |first2=Maximilian S. |last3=Oakes |first3=Patrick W. |last4=Occhipinti |first4=Patricia |last5=Gladfelter |first5=Amy S. |date=April 11, 2016 |title=Micron-scale plasma membrane curvature is recognized by the septin cytoskeleton |url=https://rupress.org/jcb/article/213/1/23/38532/Micron-scale-plasma-membrane-curvature-is |journal=Journal of Cell Biology |language=en |volume=213 |issue=1 |pages=23–32 |doi=10.1083/jcb.201512029 |issn=0021-9525|hdl=1912/7950 |hdl-access=free |pmc=4828694 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Woods |first=Benjamin L. |last2=Gladfelter |first2=Amy S. |date=February 2021 |title=The state of the septin cytoskeleton from assembly to function |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0955067420301423 |journal=Current Opinion in Cell Biology |language=en |volume=68 |pages=105–112 |doi=10.1016/j.ceb.2020.10.007|pmc=7952027 }}</ref>.  Her lab discovered septin filaments sense local cell curvature on the micron scale. This function is unique to septins amongst eukaryotic proteins and conserved from yeast to humans.  Septins monitor membrane geometry at the base of dendritic spines, the [[cleavage furrow]] and cilia, so these studies have broad importance in learning how cell shape controls cell fate. 

Here is a link to her [https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=YZO6qPoAAAAJ Google Scholar page].
